newsitem.title: GERMANY: Telekom, Daimler launch traffic navigation system.
newsitem.headline: Telekom, Daimler launch traffic navigation system.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG and Daimler-Benz AG said on Friday they would form a joint venture to develop services for automotive navigation systems based on mobile communicaitons.

The deal, to be carried out by Deutsche Telekom MobilNet GmbH, the company's mobile communications unit, and Daimler's services division Debis, marks the first major effort to offer services using satellite and mobile systems to guide traffic.

The new traffic telematics sector is expected to develop quickly into a market offering navigation assistance for big trucking fleets as well as to help direct individual drivers around tie-ups and alert authorities to traffic accidents.
"We want to be a part of this new market right from the beginning," Debis chairman Klaus Mangold told a news conference at the CeBIT technology trade fair.
"Daimler-Benz will bring its full competence into the venture and we expect the market to experience high growth rates."
The two companies expect to start offering services in the second half of this year and to have three million customers and around 200 million marks in sales by the year 2000.

Until now, telematic services have been restricted to receiving limited traffic information that is read out by a computer over a mobile phone connection using the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM) standards or so-called digital traffic maps contained on a CD-ROM installed in the dashboard.

But industry is about to take the next step forward by linking live data via the GSM network and Global Positioning System (GPS) navigational satellite system to offer services ranging from navigation and first-aid to tracking stolen cars.

In a first phase to establish such services, Telekom and Mannesmann AG set up a joint project to install the necessary telematics equipment along motorways that would gather traffic data that could be called up by individual drivers.
Although rivals in other areas of telecoms, Telekom and Mannesmann decided to cooperate in building the telematics infrastructure, but do not plan to offer joint services.
But the data that their joint project provides will be utilized by the new venture between Telekom and Debis.

The first service the two companies plan to offer is called "Tele Aid" that was developed by luxury car maker Mercedes-Benz AG and Debis and that will initially be marketed exclusively by Mercedes, the car division of Daimler-Benz.

Through a crash sensor installed in the car or a manual switch, paramedics and police will receive automatic notification of an accident and the GPS system will be able to locate the car, greatly shortening accident response time.
"This could save lives," said Lothar Hunsel, chairman of Deutsche Telekom MobilNet.

The next service planned for the end of the year is a piloting system that requires an on-board computer with CD-ROM. Using telematics data, the computer compares traffic information with the digital map and suggests an alternative route on a flip-up screen to avoid the next traffic jam.
The market for such systems already exists.
Bosch Telecom/Blaupunkt, the automotive electronics maker, has sold around 40,000 of its "Autopilot" navigation systems since entering the market in 1995 to Volkswagen AG, Audi AG and Mercedes-Benz.
"Ford and Honda will be joining soon," said Joachim Siedler, spokesman for Blaupunkt.
The company also displayed a new model, dubbed Gemini, that included GPS capabilities and could provide the kinds of services planned by Telekom and Debis.
Similar systems have been developed by Siemens AG and Motorola.
Hans-Juergen Hilgendorf, one of the two managing directors of the as yet unnamed Telekom-Debis venture, said prices for telematics hardware were falling dramatically.
"I believe that there will be products on the market for around 2,500 marks and that will be a fairly intelligent system," he said.

Telekom and Debis are targetting the new car market first and have a clear in-road at Mercedes. But if the service is to succeed they will have to remain neutral and convince other carmakers to support a product developed in part by Mercedes.
"We want to be open very quickly for other automotive manufacturers," said Mangold.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150
